case_analysis.focal_point: Whether venue for a prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 1519 can be laid in the district where the federal investigation was pending (and where the obstructive act was aimed), even if the defendant’s falsification occurred entirely in another district.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (falsifying records with intent to impede/obstruct/influence a federal investigation or proper administration of any matter within federal jurisdiction); U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3 and the Sixth Amendment Vicinage/Venue protections (implicit backdrop to the venue dispute).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues venue is improper where no conduct element of the § 1519 offense occurred, and that the Ninth Circuit’s approach—allowing venue wherever an investigation was located or where contemplated effects might be felt—dilutes Article III/Sixth Amendment venue safeguards and conflicts with the rule that venue must be tied to the location of the offense’s conduct elements rather than merely the intended or potential effects of obstruction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues venue is proper in the district of the investigation that the falsification was intended to obstruct because § 1519’s gravamen is obstruction directed at a federal matter; thus the offense is suitably prosecuted where the investigation/matter was being conducted, even if the physical act of falsifying a record happened elsewhere, since the obstructive conduct was aimed at and would operate upon that investigation.
key_precedents: Ciminelli v. United States, 598 U.S. 306 (2023) (noted in materials as granted in 2022; ultimately decided 2023 rejecting the 'right to control' theory)
United States v. Percoco, 598 U.S. 319 (2023) (appears in excerpted discussion as related context)
United States v. Alston, 974 F.2d 1206 (9th Cir. 1992) (cited in joint appendix excerpt on standards for new trial)
United States v. Kellington, 217 F.3d 1084 (9th Cir. 2000) (same context)
United States v. Del Toro-Barboza, 673 F.3d 1136 (9th Cir. 2012) (same context)
United States v. Camacho, 555 F.3d 695 (8th Cir. 2009) (same context)
United States v. Rafiekian, 991 F.3d 529 (4th Cir. 2021) (referenced in joint appendix excerpt, though not central to the § 1519 venue question)

John Roberts.reasoning: Respondent’s best point—that §1519 is obstruction aimed at protecting a federal investigation so venue should follow the investigation’s location—still runs into our locus delicti framework: we identify essential conduct elements, and here that is falsifying/altering/destroying/making a false entry, while the federal “matter within jurisdiction” is a circumstance and the “intent to impede” is mens rea. Justice Kavanaugh’s distinction from Rodriguez-Moreno is persuasive: unlike kidnapping-with-a-gun, §1519 does not contain a second conduct element occurring where the investigation sits, so treating effects as a venue hook would effectively add an atextual venue provision and erode vicinage protections. Justice Kagan’s Cabrales analogy underscores the point that downstream federal activity cannot supply venue when the defendant’s proscribed acts occurred elsewhere. A narrow holding—venue lies where the §1519 falsification (etc.) occurred absent an express congressional venue rule—best adheres to precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that §1519 is an obstruction statute whose locus should follow the targeted federal matter—fails because Article III and the Sixth Amendment fix venue where the crime was “committed,” and under Rodriguez-Moreno that means the statute’s essential conduct elements, not downstream effects. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch explain, §1519’s only proscribed conduct is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying (or making a false entry); the “intent to impede” is mens rea and the “matter within federal jurisdiction” is a circumstance/jurisdictional nexus, neither of which supplies a second conduct element in the investigation’s district. Cabrales forecloses anchoring venue in a district tied only to related federal activity when the defendant’s own acts occurred elsewhere, and reading an effects-based venue rule into §1519 would be an atextual expansion that erodes vicinage protections and invites forum shopping. Nothing in colleagues’ discussions identifies a precedent that undermines this conduct-based locus delicti analysis, so my vote remains for petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the effects-based theory that §1519 is aimed at protecting a federal “matter,” so venue should follow the investigation’s location; but as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require venue to track essential conduct, and §1519’s only proscribed conduct is the falsification/alteration/destruction (or false entry) itself. Justice Kavanaugh’s practical-consequences concern reinforces the textual and constitutional baseline: tying venue to where investigators sit would enable broad forum selection untethered to any defendant conduct in the district, diluting Article III and Sixth Amendment vicinage protections absent a clear congressional directive. Justice Thomas is also right that the “matter within federal jurisdiction” is a jurisdictional circumstance, and the intent to impede is mens rea; neither can be converted into a conduct locus without rewriting the statute and our venue precedents. I therefore see no argument that genuinely undermines the conduct-based locus delicti analysis and remain with petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best move is the effects-based theory that §1519 is aimed at protecting a federal investigation, so venue should lie where that investigation sits—but that treats anticipated impact as a substitute for an element-defining act. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, we anchor venue in the statute’s essential conduct elements; here the only conduct is falsifying/altering/destroying/making a false entry, while the federal “matter within jurisdiction” is a circumstance/jurisdictional hook and the obstructive purpose is mens rea. I also share Justice Kavanaugh’s concern that letting venue follow the investigation’s location invites prosecutor-driven forum selection that disproportionately burdens less-resourced defendants and undercuts vicinage protections. No colleague has identified a precedent that genuinely authorizes converting a circumstance/effects theory into a venue rule for a single-conduct-element statute like §1519, so I remain with petitioner.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Respondent’s best point—framed by Chief Justice Roberts—is that §1519 is an obstruction statute and therefore venue should track the district of the federal matter being obstructed, but that still treats anticipated effects and the situs of federal activity as a venue hook without textual grounding. Under Cabrales and the conduct/circumstance framework emphasized by Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett, §1519’s essential conduct is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying (or making a false entry); the “matter within federal jurisdiction” is a jurisdictional circumstance and the intent-to-impede clause is mens rea, neither of which supplies a second locus of proscribed conduct. Justice Kavanaugh’s distinction of Rodriguez-Moreno is persuasive: that case involved a continuing offense with conduct in multiple districts, whereas §1519 does not make “impacting the investigation where it sits” a conduct element, and adopting that rule would invite prosecutor-driven forum selection inconsistent with Article III and the Sixth Amendment. Absent an express venue provision, I would not infer an effects-based venue expansion from silence in a statute written against the constitutional vicinage backdrop.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the effects-based characterization of §1519 as protecting federal investigations, but that cannot supply venue absent a textual conduct hook, and Chief Justice Roberts is right to resist turning anticipated effects into locus delicti. Under Rodriguez-Moreno, we look to essential conduct elements; as Justice Thomas explains, §1519’s only proscribed conduct is falsifying/altering/destroying/making a false entry, while the “matter within federal jurisdiction” is a circumstance/jurisdictional nexus and the intent to impede is mens rea. Cabrales is therefore controlling: we do not relocate venue to a district housing related proceedings when the defendant’s criminal acts occurred elsewhere, especially where Congress has not enacted an express venue expansion. Justice Kavanaugh’s forum-shopping concern underscores why vicinage protections counsel a narrow, conduct-based venue rule here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that §1519 is aimed at protecting a federal “matter,” so venue should follow the investigation’s location—but that is an effects-based theory our venue precedents do not permit absent clear statutory direction. Chief Justice Roberts persuasively frames the “matter within federal jurisdiction” as a circumstance/jurisdictional nexus and the intent to obstruct as mens rea, leaving the only essential conduct element the falsification/alteration/destruction itself, which must anchor venue under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno. Justice Gorsuch’s emphasis that §1519 lacks the kind of second, continuing conduct element present in Rodriguez-Moreno reinforces why treating the investigation’s situs as a venue hook would improperly expand prosecutorial forum choice and dilute Article III/Sixth Amendment vicinage protections. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion identifies a precedent that authorizes venue based solely on anticipated effects in the forum, so I remain with petitioner.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the effects-based theory that §1519 protects federal investigations, so venue should track the investigation’s location; but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require venue to rest on the statute’s essential conduct elements. Section 1519’s text criminalizes the act of falsifying/altering/destroying/making a false entry; the “matter within federal jurisdiction” is a jurisdictional circumstance and the “intent to impede” is mens rea, neither of which supplies a second locus of conduct in the investigation district. Treating the investigation’s situs as a venue hook would effectively read an atextual venue-expansion into §1519 and weaken Article III and Sixth Amendment vicinage protections by permitting prosecution where the defendant committed none of the proscribed acts. Justice Kavanaugh’s distinction of Rodriguez-Moreno reinforces that, unlike a continuing offense with conduct in multiple districts, §1519 does not itself define conduct occurring where the investigation sits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the effects-based theory that §1519 protects a federal “matter,” so venue should lie where that matter is pending; but as Chief Justice Roberts explains, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require venue to track essential conduct elements, and here the only proscribed conduct is falsifying/altering/destroying (or making a false entry), not the investigation’s location. The “matter within federal jurisdiction” functions as a jurisdictional/circumstance element and the “intent to impede” is mens rea—neither supplies forum-district conduct without effectively rewriting the statute to add an atextual venue provision. I also find Justice Sotomayor’s practical-consequences point consistent with vicinage values: an effects-based rule would invite forum shopping and impose asymmetric burdens on defendants, particularly those with fewer resources, absent clear congressional authorization. Nothing in colleagues’ discussion identifies a precedent that genuinely undermines this conduct-based locus delicti analysis, so I remain with petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” and when Congress has not specified venue, we determine the locus delicti by identifying the statute’s essential conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred. Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue may lie where any part of the proscribed conduct was done, but it cannot rest solely on the location of related proceedings or anticipated effects. Section 1519 criminalizes the act of falsifying/altering/destroying a record with a specified intent; when that falsification occurs entirely in another district, the investigation’s location is at most a circumstance or effect, not an element-location that independently anchors venue. A narrow holding limiting venue to districts where the falsification (or other § 1519 conduct) occurred best preserves longstanding venue protections and avoids expanding prosecutorial discretion in a way that could undermine institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” which this Court has interpreted to mean where the offense’s essential conduct elements occurred. Under the two-step inquiry of Rodriguez-Moreno, § 1519’s essential conduct is the act of “falsif[ying],” “alter[ing],” or “mak[ing] a false entry” in a record; the remaining phrases (“with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence”) describe mens rea rather than conduct that can anchor venue. Cabrales confirms venue cannot be based merely on where related proceedings or effects are felt when the charged offense’s conduct happened elsewhere, and § 1519’s text does not make the location of the federal investigation an element. Because the alleged falsification occurred entirely outside the investigation district, venue there would dilute the Constitution’s venue/vicinage protections and expand federal prosecutorial discretion beyond the statute’s original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1519 criminalizes the act of “falsif[ying]” or “mak[ing] a false entry” in a record with a specified intent; the essential conduct element is the falsification itself, while the existence or location of a federal “matter” is a jurisdictional circumstance rather than conduct. Under Cabrales, venue must be tied to where the statutorily proscribed conduct occurred, not merely where related proceedings were pending or where the intended effects might be felt. Congress did not specify an effects-based venue rule in § 1519, and expanding venue to the district of the investigation would dilute the Article III and Sixth Amendment venue protections by allowing prosecution where no element-defining conduct happened. Practical consequences also counsel restraint: an effects-based theory would invite broad forum selection in obstruction cases whenever investigations are centralized away from the defendant’s acts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require that venue track where the crime was committed, and our cases instruct courts to identify the statute’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred. Under § 1519, the relevant conduct element is “falsif[ying]” a record; the federal “matter within [federal] jurisdiction” and the investigation’s location function as the object of the defendant’s intent, not as conduct that must occur in the forum district. As in United States v. Cabrales, venue cannot be based on downstream effects or the situs of related federal activity when the defendant’s criminal acts occurred entirely elsewhere, and Rodriguez-Moreno does not extend venue where the statute does not make effects on an investigation an element. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is pending would dilute vicinage protections and risk unfair prosecutorial forum selection, a concern that falls hardest on less-resourced defendants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” and when Congress has not specified venue we look to the offense’s “essential conduct elements” and where they occurred. Under Cabrales, venue turns on “the location of the act or acts constituting” the crime, not the situs of related proceedings or the place where downstream effects might be felt. Section 1519’s proscribed conduct is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying a record with the requisite obstructive intent, and if that conduct occurred entirely in another district, trying the case where the investigation was pending risks converting venue into an effects-based rule that dilutes constitutional venue protections. Congress can authorize broader venue expressly, but absent clear statutory direction in § 1519, the more workable and coherent reading ties venue to where the falsification occurred.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require venue to be fixed by the locus delicti, which this Court determines by identifying the offense’s essential conduct elements and locating where that conduct occurred. Under § 1519, the relevant conduct is the actus reus of “alter[ing], destroy[ing], mutilat[ing], conceal[ing], cover[ing] up, falsif[ying], or mak[ing] a false entry” in a record; the remaining language (“knowingly” and “with the intent to impede, obstruct, or influence” a federal matter) supplies mens rea rather than additional conduct that can anchor venue. Cabrales instructs that venue may not rest on the situs of related proceedings or downstream effects when the charged offense conduct occurred elsewhere, and nothing in § 1519 expressly authorizes venue where only the investigation was pending. Given the constitutional backdrop and statutory silence, the rule of lenity counsels against expanding venue beyond districts where the falsification itself occurred.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require venue where the offense was committed, which this Court has tied to the location of the crime’s conduct elements rather than the situs of effects or related proceedings. Under Cabrales, venue is improper in a district where the defendant committed no essential conduct element of the charged offense, and § 1519’s core conduct element is the act of falsifying/altering/destroying a record, which here occurred entirely outside the investigation district. Unlike Rodriguez-Moreno—where the statute contained two distinct conduct elements and part of the offense (the continuing kidnapping) occurred in the trial district—§ 1519 does not make the existence/location of the federal investigation a conduct element, but instead supplies the jurisdictional nexus and intent object. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is pending would risk diluting vicinage protections and create practical, prosecutor-driven forum selection untethered to where the defendant acted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1519 contains no venue provision, so venue turns on the locus delicti: “the nature of the crime alleged and the location of the act or acts constituting it.” United States v. Cabrales, 524 U.S. 1, 6–7 (1998) (quoting Anderson). Applying Rodriguez-Moreno’s framework, we identify §1519’s essential conduct element as the act of “falsif[ying]” or “mak[ing] a false entry” in a record; the existence or location of a federal “matter within the jurisdiction” and the defendant’s intent to impede it are circumstance/mental-state elements that do not themselves supply venue. Allowing venue wherever an investigation is pending would untether prosecution from where the defendant’s conduct occurred and dilute Article III and Sixth Amendment venue safeguards absent clear congressional direction, especially where (as here) all falsification occurred in another district.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Because 18 U.S.C. § 1519 contains no venue clause, Article III and the Sixth Amendment require venue to be tied to “the location of the act or acts constituting” the offense. Under Rodriguez-Moreno, venue turns on the statute’s “essential conduct elements,” and § 1519’s conduct element is the falsification/alteration/destruction of records; the existence or location of a federal investigation is, at most, a jurisdictional or circumstance element, while intent to obstruct is mens rea and cannot supply venue. Allowing venue wherever the investigation was pending would dilute vicinage protections by converting intended effects into a venue hook, contrary to the conduct-based approach reflected in Anderson and reinforced by the distinction between conduct and circumstance elements in Rodriguez-Moreno. Practical consequences also counsel restraint: a broad effects-based rule risks forum shopping and imposes unfair burdens on defendants whose only conduct occurred entirely in another district.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether venue for a prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 1519 is proper in the district where the federal investigation occurred (or was contemplated to be affected) even if all of the defendant’s allegedly obstructive acts took place in a different district.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3 and the Sixth Amendment Vicinage/Venue Clauses; Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 18; and 18 U.S.C. § 1519 (Sarbanes–Oxley anti-shredding/obstruction statute).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues venue is unconstitutional and statutorily improper where no element-conduct occurred in the charging district: § 1519’s actus reus is the falsification/destruction/concealment of records, and that conduct happened outside the chosen venue; an intent to obstruct a federal investigation that is located elsewhere cannot by itself create venue because the Constitution requires trial where the crime was committed, meaning where essential conduct elements occurred, not where effects were merely contemplated or where the government later investigates. Petitioner contends the Ninth Circuit’s approach effectively allows venue to be manufactured by the government’s choice of investigative location and collapses venue into an effects-based theory untethered from the defendant’s conduct, contrary to this Court’s venue jurisprudence.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues venue is proper in the district of the federal investigation at which the obstructive conduct was directed because § 1519 criminalizes falsification done with the specific intent to obstruct a matter within federal jurisdiction; when the defendant’s objective is to obstruct an investigation in a particular district, the offense is ‘committed’ there in a venue-relevant sense. In the government’s view, § 1519 is an obstruction statute oriented to protecting the integrity of federal proceedings/matters, so the locus of the targeted investigation provides an appropriate and constitutionally permissible venue even if the physical falsification occurred elsewhere.

United States v. Percoco, 13 F.4th 158 (2d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Kellington, 217 F.3d 1084 (9th Cir. 2000)
United States v. Alston, 974 F.2d 1206 (9th Cir. 1992)
United States v. Del Toro-Barboza, 673 F.3d 1136 (9th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Camacho, 555 F.3d 695 (8th Cir. 2009)
United States v. Rafiekian, 991 F.3d 529 (4th Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: The Government’s best argument—that § 1519’s federal “matter” and intent-to-impede language makes the offense effectively effects-based, permitting venue where the investigation sits—still treats a circumstance/mens rea nexus as if it were an essential conduct element, contrary to Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno. As Justice Kagan persuasively underscores, anchoring venue to the Government’s investigative situs would invite manufactured venue and forum shopping untethered to the defendant’s acts, undermining Article III and the Sixth Amendment’s structural protections. Justice Alito’s practical-consequences point reinforces that our narrowest legitimate holding is simply that, where all falsification/destruction/concealment occurred outside the charging district and no conduct element occurred there, venue is improper. Precedents like Anderson do not change the analysis because they do not authorize relocating venue based solely on governmental activity absent statutory text making the offense continuing or otherwise specifying broader venue.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that § 1519 targets interference with a federal “matter,” so venue should follow the investigation’s situs; but that reads a circumstance and intent clause as if it were an additional conduct element. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, our locus-delicti framework (Cabrales; Rodriguez-Moreno) anchors venue to where the defendant’s essential conduct occurred, and here the only conduct Congress criminalized is falsifying/destroying/concealing records—acts completed where the defendant acted, not where the Government later investigates. Justice Kagan’s forum-manufacture concern underscores why an investigation-based venue rule cannot be reconciled with Article III and the Sixth Amendment absent a clear textual venue expansion or a true continuing-offense statute. Nothing in § 1519 (or § 3237(a) on these facts) supplies that clear authorization, so the constitutional baseline controls.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best theory—venue where the federal “matter” is investigated because § 1519 targets interference with that matter—still treats a circumstance/mens rea hook as if it were conduct, which Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno do not allow. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about government-manufactured venue is especially persuasive as a practical consequence: if venue follows investigative situs, the Executive can effectively pick its forum without any defendant act there, defeating the structural protections of Article III, the Sixth Amendment, and Rule 18. Nothing in § 1519’s text clearly makes this a continuing offense or otherwise authorizes venue absent conduct in the district, and § 3237(a) cannot supply that missing link on these facts. I therefore remain with petitioner and would hold venue improper where all falsification/destruction/concealment occurred elsewhere.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s best theory—that § 1519 is effectively effects-based because it targets obstruction of a federal “matter,” so venue should follow the investigation—runs into the same wall as Cabrales: the federal-matter nexus is a circumstance/intent feature, not an essential conduct element occurring wherever agents later work. Justice Kagan’s framing is especially persuasive to me: the “matter” language identifies the object of the falsification/destruction, it does not create a second locus of criminal conduct in the investigation district. Chief Justice Roberts’s warning about manufactured venue underscores the real-world harm here—forum shopping and burdensome distant trials fall hardest on defendants with limited means, undermining the structural and fairness purposes of the Venue and Vicinage Clauses and Rule 18. Nothing in § 1519 or § 3237(a) clearly converts this into a continuing offense absent multi-district defendant conduct, so venue is improper where only government activity occurred.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s best point is that § 1519 targets obstruction of a federal “matter,” so venue should lie where that matter is administered or investigated; but that treats the statute’s object (and the defendant’s intent about it) as if it were conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, tying venue to the investigation’s situs allows government-manufactured venue and forum shopping, which our essential-conduct framework (Cabrales; Rodriguez-Moreno) is designed to prevent by anchoring venue in where the defendant’s falsifying/destroying/concealing occurred. Justice Alito’s practical-consequences concern confirms the workability problem: an investigation-based rule would be unpredictable and executive-controlled rather than statute-controlled. Nothing in § 1519’s text or § 3237(a) clearly makes this a continuing offense across districts absent any defendant act in the charging district, so the constitutional and Rule 18 baseline controls.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—that § 1519 targets interference with a federal “investigation” or “matter within the jurisdiction,” so venue should lie where that matter sits—still treats an object/intent feature as if it were conduct. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno require us to identify the statute’s essential conduct elements, and here those are only falsifying/destroying/concealing a record, which occur where the defendant acts, not where the Government later investigates. Justice Kagan’s manufactured-venue concern follows from the same constitutional structure: if investigative situs alone sufficed, the Executive could pick venue by choosing where to open a file, contrary to Article III, the Sixth Amendment, and Rule 18 absent clear statutory authorization. Neither § 1519’s text nor § 3237(a) supplies that authorization on these facts because no relevant conduct occurred in the charging district, so I remain with petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s best point remains that § 1519’s “intent to impede … any matter” could be read to place the offense where the federal matter is investigated, but under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno that “matter” is a circumstance/object of the intent, not an essential conduct element that can supply venue absent any defendant act in the charging district. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on manufactured venue is decisive for me as an institutional and practical matter: tying venue to the Executive’s investigative situs invites forum shopping and undermines the Article III and Sixth Amendment structural protections that Rule 18 reflects. Nothing in § 1519’s text clearly designates an effects-based or continuing-offense venue rule, and § 3237(a) cannot do the work without multi-district conduct. I therefore agree with Justice Thomas that the locus delicti is where the falsification/destruction/concealment occurred, and venue in the investigation district is improper on these facts.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Government’s best point remains that § 1519’s “investigation”/“matter within the jurisdiction” language could be read to supply a venue locus where that matter is pursued, but under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno venue must be anchored in essential conduct elements, not jurisdictional or intent-related circumstances. Chief Justice Roberts’s concern about manufactured venue is decisive for me: if investigative situs alone sufficed, the Executive could effectively select venue untethered to any defendant act, in tension with Article III, the Sixth Amendment, and Rule 18. No colleague has identified statutory text in § 1519 that clearly makes this a continuing offense, and § 3237(a) cannot expand venue absent multi-district conduct. Justice Kagan’s workability point reinforces that an investigation-based rule would be both malleable and constitutionally suspect, so venue is improper on these facts where all falsification/destruction/concealment occurred elsewhere.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s best theory—that § 1519’s “intent to impede” a federal “matter” makes venue proper where investigators sit—still treats contemplated effects or governmental activity as a stand-in for defendant conduct, which Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno do not permit. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about manufactured venue is especially persuasive on pragmatic and fairness grounds: if venue can follow the Government’s investigative choice, defendants (particularly those with limited resources) can be hauled far from where their alleged acts occurred, undermining the structural protections of Article III and the Sixth Amendment. Justice Kagan’s workability concern reinforces that this approach would be difficult to administer and invite forum shopping without any clear congressional authorization. Because § 1519’s essential conduct is falsifying/destroying/concealing records, and none occurred in the charging district on these facts, venue there is improper.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require prosecution where the crime was “committed,” which this Court has tied to the location of the offense’s essential conduct elements rather than mere circumstance or intent. Under the two-step framework of Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, § 1519’s essential conduct is the falsification/destruction/concealment of a record; the “intent to impede” a federal matter is a mental-state element that does not itself supply venue in a district where no conduct occurred. Allowing venue where the investigation happened to be located would risk government-manufactured venue and undermine the structural protections the Venue and Vicinage Clauses secure, absent a clear congressional directive to treat the offense as continuing or effects-based (cf. Fed. R. Crim. P. 18; 18 U.S.C. § 3237(a)). A narrow ruling holding venue improper on these facts preserves constitutional limits without narrowing § 1519’s substantive reach.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was “committed,” which turns on the location of the offense’s essential conduct elements rather than the situs of a related investigation or contemplated effects. Under this Court’s framework, courts must identify the conduct constituting the offense and then locate where that conduct occurred; § 1519’s essential conduct is the falsification/destruction/concealment of records, while the “intent to impede” a federal matter is a mens rea element that does not itself supply venue. United States v. Cabrales, 524 U.S. 1 (1998), and United States v. Rodriguez-Moreno, 526 U.S. 275 (1999), reject venue theories that rest on downstream effects or the government’s choice of where to investigate when the defendant’s conduct occurred elsewhere. Reading § 1519 to permit venue in the investigation’s district would effectively allow prosecutors to manufacture venue untethered from the defendant’s acts, contrary to the Constitution’s text and Rule 18’s district-of-the-offense command.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “where the crime shall have been committed,” and this Court’s venue cases direct us to identify the statute’s essential conduct elements and locate where that conduct occurred. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the proscribed conduct is the destruction, alteration, or falsification of records; the “matter within the jurisdiction” language and the intent to impede it are circumstance/mental-state components that do not themselves create venue where no act was performed. Cabrales holds venue cannot rest on jurisdictional or effects-based theories when the defendant’s laundering conduct occurred entirely elsewhere, and allowing venue in the investigation district here would similarly let the Government manufacture venue by choosing where to investigate, undermining Rule 18’s district-of-offense principle. Practical consequences also counsel against the Government’s rule because it invites forum shopping and burdens defendants with trials far from where their conduct occurred.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Because § 1519 contains no venue provision, the Constitution’s venue and vicinage commands (Art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Sixth Amendment) require locating the “locus delicti” by identifying the statute’s “essential conduct elements” and where those acts occurred. Under Rodriguez-Moreno and Anderson, the essential conduct in § 1519 is the falsification/destruction/concealment of records; the federal-jurisdiction/intent-to-obstruct component is a circumstance element that cannot, standing alone, manufacture venue in a distant district where no conduct occurred. Allowing venue wherever the government later investigates (or where effects are contemplated) invites forum shopping and imposes serious, unfair burdens on defendants—especially those with limited means—contrary to Rule 18’s emphasis on prosecution in the district where the offense was committed. On this record, venue is improper in the investigation district if all obstructive acts happened elsewhere.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “in the State and district wherein the crime shall have been committed,” and our venue cases implement that by asking where the statute’s essential conduct elements occurred. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1519, the proscribed conduct is the falsification/destruction/concealment of records; the federal-jurisdictional “matter” and the intent to obstruct it describe the object of the conduct, not additional conduct occurring where investigators later work. Cabrales holds that venue cannot be based on out-of-district effects or a jurisdictional nexus when the defendant’s relevant conduct happened elsewhere, and permitting venue where the investigation sits risks government-manufactured venue and poor workability. Nothing in § 1519’s text makes the place of the contemplated investigation an element-locus, and Rule 18’s default (“prosecute an offense in a district where the offense was committed”) points the same way absent a clear statutory venue expansion.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial “wherein the crime shall have been committed,” and this Court has instructed that venue turns on the locus delicti—“the conduct constituting the offense”—by identifying the statute’s essential conduct elements and locating where they occurred. United States v. Rodriguez-Moreno, 526 U.S. 275, 279–80 (1999); United States v. Anderson, 328 U.S. 699, 703 (1946). Under § 1519, the essential conduct element is the act of falsifying/destroying/concealing a record; the statute’s reference to intent to impede a federal matter describes mens rea, not an additional conduct element that can relocate venue to wherever the government investigates or feels an intended effect. Allowing venue in the investigation’s district would convert the constitutional venue guarantee into an effects-based or government-controlled rule, inviting forum shopping and diluting the structural protection the Vicinage/Venue Clauses were designed to secure.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Because § 1519 contains no venue provision, Article III, § 2 and the Sixth Amendment require venue where the crime was “committed,” which this Court has tied to the location of the offense’s “essential conduct elements.” Under Rodriguez-Moreno, the intent-to-obstruct-a-federal-matter component functions as a circumstance/mental-state element, while the core conduct—“falsif[ying],” “destroy[ing],” or “conceal[ing]” a record—supplies the relevant conduct for venue purposes and occurred only in the petitioner’s district. Allowing venue in the district of the investigation would effectively permit effects- or government-chosen-investigative-location venue untethered to defendant conduct, undermining the Constitution’s vicinage protections and creating practical risks of forum manipulation inconsistent with Rule 18’s district-of-offense baseline. The government remains able to prosecute where the falsification occurred (or where Congress has expressly authorized broader venue), but absent such authorization, precedent and tradition counsel a narrower, conduct-based venue rule here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III and the Sixth Amendment require trial in the State and district where the crime was "committed," and our cases instruct that venue turns on the location of the offense’s essential conduct elements, not merely the place of intended effects or related governmental activity. Under § 1519’s text, the sole conduct element is the knowing falsification/destruction/concealment of a record; the reference to an “investigation” or “matter within the jurisdiction” of a federal agency functions as a mens rea/targeting requirement, not an additional conduct element that occurs where the government investigates. Applying Anderson and Rodriguez-Moreno, and consistent with Cabrales’s rejection of effects- or circumstance-only venue, prosecution must lie where the falsification occurred, not where a federal investigation later happens to be located. Allowing venue in the investigation’s district would untether venue from the defendant’s acts and permit governmental manufacture of venue, in tension with the constitutional vicinage protections and Rule 18’s presumption of prosecution in the district of the offense.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Venue and Vicinage Clauses (U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3; Sixth Amendment) and Rule 18 require trial where the crime was committed, which this Court has tied to the location of the offense’s “essential conduct elements.” Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno’s two-step framework, § 1519’s essential conduct is the falsification/destruction/concealment act, while the “intent to obstruct” language is mens rea and cannot alone supply venue in a different district. Allowing venue wherever a federal investigation occurred (or was contemplated) would effectively permit the government to manufacture venue based on investigative choices and would undermine procedural fairness by forcing defendants to stand trial far from where their conduct occurred. Because all alleged obstructive acts happened outside the charging district, venue there is improper absent a statutory basis making § 1519 a continuing offense under § 3237(a) grounded in conduct occurring in that district.
